how large language models work attention
a: Large Language Models (LLMs) are artificial neural networks trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like text. They are based on the transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need. The core mechanism is self-attention, which allows the model to weigh the importance of different words in the input when generating each output word. LLMs are trained through next-token prediction: given a sequence of words, the model learns to predict the next most likely word. Through this process on billions of text examples, the model develops a statistical understanding of language patterns, grammar, facts, and reasoning. The training process has two main stages: pretraining on large public text corpora (books, websites, articles), followed by fine-tuning on curated datasets with human feedback (RLHF - Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback). Key architectural components include: tokenization (splitting text into tokens), embedding layers (converting tokens to vectors), multiple transformer layers with self-attention and feed-forward networks, and an output layer that predicts the next token probability distribution. The model size ranges from billions to trillions of parameters (the weights learned during training). Prominent examples include GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama. Despite their capabilities, LLMs have limitations: they can produce incorrect information (hallucination), have no true understanding or consciousness, can reflect biases in their training data, and require substantial computational resources.
